question: What are some safety precautions to consider when operating near jet-powered airplanes on the ground?

correct_answers.text: Avoid standing near the engine intake to prevent being pulled in.
Be cautious of hot and fast-moving exhaust that can blow a person down.
Exercise caution during taxi to avoid jet blast affecting ground equipment.

wrong_answers.text: Stand close to the engine intake for better visibility.
Ignore the exhaust as it is not a safety concern.
Increase power rapidly to start moving quickly.
Jet engines are safe at idle and pose no threat.
Jet blast only affects large equipment, not small items.
There is no need for caution when taxiing into parking areas.
Debris on the ground is not a concern for jet engines.
Jet engines have visible propellers to indicate they are running.

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 16: Transition to Jet-Powered Airplanes Introduction

question: Which of the following are true regarding turbofan engine design and operation?

correct_answers.text: The bypass ratio compares the amount of air bypassing the core to the amount compressed for combustion
Each turbine sub-section connects to a specific compressor sub-section via a split-spool shaft
The turbofan engine improves acceleration and decreases takeoff roll compared to a turbojet

wrong_answers.text: The first compressor stage has the smallest diameter and thinnest blades
Igniters continuously fire throughout engine operation to sustain combustion
A turbojet diverts bypass air around the engine core to produce additional thrust
The turbofan engine is most efficient at higher altitudes compared to lower altitudes
The turbine section drives the compressor by extracting all available energy from the airflow
Bypass air in a turbofan is hotter and faster than the core exhaust gas
The compressor section in a turbofan is a single unified spool with no sub-sections
Higher bypass ratio means more air is directed through the combustion chamber

source: AFH Chapter 16, Section 16.2: Jet Engine Basics

question: In a jet engine, which of the following statements accurately describe how thrust is controlled and indicated on the flight deck?

correct_answers.text: The amount of fuel injected into the combustion chamber controls thrust.
Thrust levers link to a fuel control and/or electronic engine computer that meters fuel flow.
Flight deck indications for rotation speed read as percent of rpm rather than actual rpm.

wrong_answers.text: Thrust is primarily controlled by adjusting the compressor blade angle.
Thrust levers directly control the physical position of the turbine blades.
Flight deck indications for rotation speed display actual rpm values in the thousands.
Engine power is set by directly adjusting the exhaust nozzle diameter.
Fuel flow is manually adjusted by the pilot using a separate lever.
Thrust is controlled by varying the amount of air entering the engine.
Engine indications typically show only fuel pressure and oil temperature.
The thrust lever directly regulates the bypass ratio in turbofan engines.

question: Regarding the operation and limitations of jet engines, which of the following statements are true?

correct_answers.text: Exceeding temperature or rpm limits, even for a few seconds, may result in serious damage to turbine blades and other components.
The pilot should monitor the temperature of turbine gases and rotation speeds as needed.
Modern aircraft are designed to prevent exceedances and alert the pilot of an impending or actual exceedance.

wrong_answers.text: Brief exceedances of temperature or rpm limits are generally harmless to jet engines.
Only older aircraft designs incorporate systems to prevent engine exceedances.
Pilots primarily monitor oil pressure and hydraulic fluid levels for engine health.
Engine damage from exceedances is typically limited to minor cosmetic issues.
Modern aircraft rely solely on pilot vigilance to prevent engine limit exceedances.
Exceeding limits only causes damage if sustained for several minutes.
Turbine gas temperature is not a critical parameter for pilot monitoring.
Engine rotation speeds are automatically adjusted and do not require pilot monitoring.

question: When operating a jet engine, what is true about the relationship between thrust levers, RPM, and engine efficiency?

correct_answers.text: Thrust output changes much more per increment of throttle movement at high engine speeds.
Jets operate most efficiently in the 85 percent to 100 percent rpm range.
At idle rpm of approximately 55 percent to 60 percent, jet engines produce a relatively small amount of thrust.

wrong_answers.text: Thrust output changes linearly with throttle movement across all engine speeds.
Jet engines are most efficient at idle rpm settings.
A small thrust lever movement at low rpm significantly increases power output.
Idle rpm typically produces the maximum available thrust for taxiing.
The most efficient rpm range for jets is between 30 percent and 50 percent.
Thrust lever movement has a greater effect on power output at low engine speeds.
An increase from 90 to 100 percent rpm provides only a negligible thrust increase.
Jet engines produce maximum thrust at 55 percent rpm.

question: Which statements accurately describe the acceleration characteristics and efficiency factors of jet engines?

correct_answers.text: Acceleration of a jet engine from idle to full power is usually much slower than a piston engine.
Pilots should anticipate the need for adding power from low power settings.
The efficiency of the jet engine increases in the cold temperatures found at high altitudes.

wrong_answers.text: Jet engines accelerate from idle to full power more rapidly than piston engines.
Pilots can react instantly to power demands due to rapid jet engine acceleration.
Jet engine efficiency decreases in cold temperatures and at high altitudes.
Fuel consumption of jet engines increases as outside air temperature decreases.
Transition to full power in a jet engine typically takes less than 2 seconds.
Jet engine efficiency is unaffected by ambient temperature or altitude.
Pilots should avoid anticipating power needs, as the engine responds quickly.
Fuel consumption is highest in cold, high-altitude conditions.

question: What are some challenges pilots face when transitioning to jet-powered airplanes due to the absence of propeller drag?

correct_answers.text: Difficulty in slowing down the airplane quickly
Jet engines still produce forward thrust at idle
Aerodynamically clean airframe contributes to less drag

wrong_answers.text: Immediate decrease in altitude when throttles are closed
Jet engines produce significant drag at idle
Propellers create more drag in jets
Jets require less distance to lose airspeed
Jets have more drag than piston-powered airplanes
Jets slow down faster than piston-powered airplanes

question: What are the maximum operating speeds in jet airplanes referred to as?

correct_answers.text: VMO
MMO
Mach number

question: What happens when a jet airplane exceeds its maximum operating Mach number (MMO)?

correct_answers.text: Severe buffeting
Possible loss of control
Mach tuck

question: Which statements correctly describe the characteristics of Mach buffet at low-speed cruise?

correct_answers.text: The shock wave does not move as far aft as it does in high-speed cruise
The separated flow acts over a larger portion of the chord
The effect on aircraft control is more significant than in high-speed cruise

wrong_answers.text: The shock wave moves further aft than in high-speed cruise
The separated flow acts over a smaller portion of the chord
The buffet produces only a slight buzz due to limited surface area affected
Mach buffet at low speed is caused by a stall rather than shock wave separation
The airflow over the upper wing surface remains subsonic throughout low-speed cruise
Low-speed Mach buffet is unaffected by the angle of attack required to maintain flight
The shock wave position is identical between low-speed and high-speed cruise conditions
Airflow separation at low-speed cruise occurs on the lower surface of the wing

question: Which statements accurately describe the concept of 'coffin corner' and the aerodynamic ceiling?

correct_answers.text: Flying faster than MMO at the aerodynamic ceiling leads to high-speed Mach buffet
Flying slower at the aerodynamic ceiling requires an AOA that causes low-speed Mach buffet
An increase in load factor raises the low-end buffet speed, reducing the available margin

wrong_answers.text: Coffin corner is the altitude where the airplane can safely accelerate beyond MMO
The aerodynamic ceiling is determined by engine thrust limitations rather than buffet onset
At coffin corner, low-speed buffet is eliminated by reducing angle of attack
An increase in G-load lowers the low-end buffet speed, expanding the safe flight envelope
The manufacturer's recommended turbulence penetration speed minimizes the margin between high- and low-speed buffets
Flying at MMO at the aerodynamic ceiling provides a large margin for maneuvering
Coffin corner only applies to propeller-driven aircraft operating at high altitudes
High-speed Mach buffet at coffin corner results from airflow separation on the lower wing surface

subjects: Aerodynamic Ceiling and Load Factor Effects

question: What are some characteristics of jet airplane wings that affect low-speed flight?

correct_answers.text: Lower aspect ratio
Thin airfoil shape
Swept wing design

question: What are some characteristics of swept wing jet airplanes during stalls?

correct_answers.text: Gradual buildup of lift
Less-defined maximum coefficient of lift
High drag at high-lift conditions

wrong_answers.text: Stick shakers activate at 90% stall speed
No need for pitch trim during recovery

question: What modifications can prevent swept wing airplanes from stalling at the wingtips?

correct_answers.text: Wing twist
Changes in airfoil section
Inclusion of vortex generators

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 16: Transition to Jet-Powered Airplanes Introduction

question: What actions should a pilot take when encountering a stall warning in a jet airplane?

correct_answers.text: Apply nose-down input
Use pitch trim if necessary
Roll wings level

correct_answers.text: To spoil lift
To increase drag

correct_answers.text: Target reversers
Cascade reversers
Clamshell doors

correct_answers.text: About 45° from straight ahead
Not completely reversed
Partially redirected

question: What factors should be considered when using reverse thrust on landing?

correct_answers.text: Runway surface conditions
Directional control
Nose-up pitch effect

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 16: Transition to Jet-Powered Airplanes Introduction

question: What are the general sensations pilots transitioning into jet-powered airplanes may notice?

correct_answers.text: Response differences
Increased control sensitivity
Increased tempo of flight

wrong_answers.text: Slower airspeed changes in some flight conditions
More gradual deceleration when thrust is reduced
Less drag at low power settings
Varying power settings due to significant weight changes
Greater reliance on flight instruments at high pitch attitudes
A tendency to overcontrol pitch during initial training flights

question: Which statements accurately describe the aerodynamic and thrust characteristics of jet airplanes compared to propeller airplanes?

correct_answers.text: More gradual deceleration when thrust is reduced due to clean aerodynamic design.
Less drag at low power settings due to the lack of propeller effects.
Reduced ability to accelerate at high altitudes due to reduced available thrust.

wrong_answers.text: Lack of effective slipstream over lifting and control surfaces.
Pitching tendency with the lowering of flaps.
The need to change power settings smoothly.
Reliance on airspeed trend information for power required.
A tendency to overcontrol pitch during initial training.
The use of small, intermittent applications of pitch trim.

question: What are key techniques or considerations for pilots to master when managing controls and power in a jet airplane?

correct_answers.text: Changing power settings smoothly.
Using several small, intermittent applications of pitch trim.
Learning when to use available drag devices appropriately to slow the airplane.

wrong_answers.text: Reduced ability to accelerate at high altitudes.
Greater reliance on flight instruments at high pitch attitudes.
Control surfaces being less effective at higher speeds.
Holding the trim button for longer periods of time.
Gripping the yoke with the hand at high speeds.

question: Regarding the generic jet airplane takeoff and climb procedures described in the Airplane Flying Handbook, which of the following statements are correct?

correct_answers.text: The information presented is generic in nature and assumes a two-pilot crew
If the AFM procedures for a specific airplane conflict with the generic information, the AFM procedures take precedence
If FAA-approved procedures developed for a specific air operator differ from the generic procedures, the operator's FAA-approved procedures take precedence

wrong_answers.text: The generic procedures apply universally and override all AFM procedures
Most civilian jet airplanes require a minimum flight crew of three pilots
The generic procedures were developed specifically for military jet operations
AFM procedures may be disregarded if they conflict with the generic handbook information
The generic information assumes a single-pilot crew for all civilian jet operations
FAA-approved training center procedures must always defer to the generic handbook procedures
Operator-specific FAA-approved procedures are only advisory and the generic procedures take precedence
The handbook procedures take precedence over all FAA-approved air operator procedures

source: AFH Chapter 16, Section 16.12: Jet Airplane Takeoff and Climb

question: Which of the following V-speeds are critical for a jet airplane's takeoff performance?

correct_answers.text: V1 —critical engine failure speed or takeoff decision speed
VR —rotation speed
V2 —takeoff safety speed

wrong_answers.text: VEF —speed used during certification for engine failure

question: What should be done before releasing the brakes during a takeoff roll on a limited runway?

correct_answers.text: Check engine instruments for proper operation
Align airplane in the center of the runway
Bring thrust levers to specified power setting

question: What is the primary responsibility of the pilot not flying during the takeoff roll?

correct_answers.text: Monitor aircraft systems
Call out proper V speeds
Cross-check takeoff data

question: What should be computed prior to each takeoff?

correct_answers.text: Takeoff power settings
V1/VR and V2 speeds
Required field length

correct_answers.text: No torque-produced yawing
Maintaining centerline
Keeping wings level

question: According to the AFH, which of the following are valid reasons that could trigger a rejected takeoff (RTO)?

correct_answers.text: Engine failure during the takeoff roll
Bird strike during the takeoff roll
Direct instructions from the governing ATC authority

wrong_answers.text: Passenger request to return to the gate
Cabin crew completing safety briefing late
Autopilot failing to engage after liftoff
Fuel quantity gauge fluctuation at cruise altitude
Gear warning light illuminating after landing
Loss of cabin pressure at cruise altitude

question: Which of the following factors can degrade stopping performance during a rejected takeoff, according to the AFH?

correct_answers.text: Natural contaminants such as standing water, snow, slush, or ice
Inoperative anti-skid system
Underinflated or failing tires

wrong_answers.text: Use of autopilot during the takeoff roll
Passenger weight distribution in the cabin
Use of engine bleed air for cabin pressurization at cruise
Flap position set to maximum for landing

question: Regarding the go/no-go decision and V1, which of the following statements are correct according to the AFH?

correct_answers.text: The go/no-go decision should be made before V1 so that deceleration can begin no later than V1
Delaying the RTO maneuver by just one second beyond V1 increases speed by 4 to 6 knots on average
If braking has not begun by V1, the decision to continue the takeoff is made by default

wrong_answers.text: V1 is the speed at which the aircraft becomes airborne
A rejected takeoff can be safely initiated at any speed below VR
Crews typically require less than one second to identify and execute an RTO
Reverse thrust is included in FAA-approved stopping distance calculations
The go/no-go decision may be made up to five seconds after V1
High-speed aborts below 80 knots account for the majority of RTO overrun accidents
FAA-approved takeoff data assumes a wet runway for conservatism
Delaying the RTO by two seconds beyond V1 has no significant effect on stopping distance

question: According to the AFH, which of the following correctly describe the expanded regulatory definition of V1?

correct_answers.text: V1 is the maximum speed by which a rejected takeoff assures a safe stop within the remaining runway or runway and stopway
V1 is the minimum speed that assures a takeoff can be safely completed after failure of the most critical engine
V1 is the single speed permitting a successful stop or continued takeoff when operating at minimum allowable field length for a particular weight

wrong_answers.text: V1 is the speed at which the nose wheel lifts off the runway
V1 is the speed at which the aircraft achieves a positive rate of climb
V1 is always equal to VR for transport category aircraft
V1 is the speed at which full rudder authority is first available
V1 is the speed used to compute maximum landing distance
V1 is defined solely by aircraft gross weight without regard to runway length
V1 is the speed at which reverse thrust becomes effective
V1 is the speed at which the autopilot must be engaged for a continued takeoff

question: According to the AFH, which of the following statements about FAA-approved takeoff performance data and RTO statistics are accurate?

correct_answers.text: FAA-approved takeoff data is based on aircraft performance demonstrated using a clean, dry runway
Reverse thrust is not used to compute stopping distance in FAA-approved takeoff data
High-speed aborts above 120 knots account for the vast majority of RTO overrun accidents despite representing only 2 percent of rejected takeoffs

wrong_answers.text: FAA-approved takeoff data includes a wet runway safety margin by regulation
Reverse thrust is the primary factor used to compute FAA-approved stopping distance
The majority of RTO overrun accidents occur at speeds below 80 knots
High-speed aborts above 120 knots represent the majority of all rejected takeoffs
FAA-approved takeoff data assumes maximum crosswind conditions for conservatism

Grooved runways are assumed in all FAA-approved stopping distance calculations
Anti-skid system performance is excluded from all FAA-approved takeoff data

Achieve V2 speed at 35 feet AGL
Maintain a constant takeoff pitch attitude regardless of weight

wrong_answers.text: Rotate to takeoff pitch attitude too soon to extend takeoff roll

Achieve V2 speed at 50 feet AGL

Ignore VR and focus on VLOF

Have three descent segments with two speed reductions.

Terrain considerations

question: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, which statements accurately describe the determination and considerations for jet engine landing distances?

correct_answers.text: The landing profile is the horizontal distance required to land and come to a complete stop from a point 50 feet above the landing surface.
Manufacturers determine baseline landing distance on a dry, level runway at standard temperatures without using thrust reversers.

wrong_answers.text: Certified landing distances are established by utilizing reverse thrust.

Manufacturers determine baseline landing distance using auto-land systems.

VREF — 1.3 times the stall speed in the landing configuration

VY — best rate of climb speed

question: What are some reasons why jet airplanes are less forgiving than piston-engine airplanes during approaches?

correct_answers.text: Jet engine response at low rpm is slower.
There is no propeller slipstream to produce immediate extra lift.
Drag increases faster than lift at low speeds.

wrong_answers.text: Jet airplanes have a smaller variety of glidepath angles.
Jet airplanes have a lower approach speed than propeller airplanes.
Propeller airplanes require more stable approaches.
Jet airplanes can salvage a misjudged glidepath with a burst of power.
Propeller slipstream lowers the power-on stall speed in jets.
Jet airplanes have a tendency to re-acquire original speed easily.
Jet airplanes are lighter than propeller airplanes.
Jet airplanes have a larger window for speed differentials.

question: What are the characteristics of jet airplanes that necessitate a stabilized approach?

correct_answers.text: Jet airplanes are consistently heavier and have faster approach speeds.
There is little tendency for jet airplanes to re-acquire original speed.
Jet airplane wings have a large increase in drag in the approach configuration.

wrong_answers.text: Jet airplanes have a smaller increase in drag during approach.
Jet airplanes can easily adjust speed without planning.
Jet airplanes have a consistent tendency to re-acquire speed.
Jet airplanes require less force to overcome momentum.
Jet airplanes have a slower approach speed than propeller airplanes.
Jet airplanes can rely on propeller slipstream for lift.
Jet airplanes have a quick engine response at low rpm.
Jet airplanes can easily salvage a misjudged glidepath.

question: Which of the following are key elements of a stabilized approach in a jet-powered airplane?

correct_answers.text: The airplane should be in the landing configuration by 1,000 feet AGL.
The airplane should be on profile before descending below 1,000 feet AGL.
Indicated airspeed should be between zero and 10 knots above the target airspeed by 500 feet AGL.

wrong_answers.text: The airplane should be in the landing configuration by 500 feet AGL.
A go-around should be initiated if not stabilized by 1,000 feet AGL.
The optimum glidepath angle should be about 5 degrees.
Typical descent rates fall between 300 and 400 feet per minute.
The target touchdown zone is approximately 500 feet down the runway.
Runway length limitations assume a 100-foot threshold height.
Fuel balancing is only required after landing.
Indicated airspeed should be between 10 and 20 knots above target airspeed by 500 feet AGL.

question: What are the consequences of carrying excess approach speed in a jet airplane?

Increased distance to touchdown

Reduce thrust smoothly to idle
Plan for a deliberate touchdown

wrong_answers.text: Hold off the airplane to dissipate speed
Initiate flare with a rapid pitch increase
Use maximum flaps for all landings
Focus solely on speed bleed off

correct_answers.text: Increased runway usage
Potential tail strike
Excessive pitch attitude

question: Which statements accurately describe the forces available for stopping a jet airplane during rollout?

correct_answers.text: Brakes are the most important stopping force for most landings.
Reverse thrust and aerodynamic drag are most effective at high speeds.
Reverse thrust and aerodynamic drag are not affected by runway surface conditions.

wrong_answers.text: Brakes are most effective at high speeds.

Spoilers are considered one of the three primary stopping forces.
On slippery runways, wheel braking is always the dominant stopping force.
The effectiveness of reverse thrust decreases on dry runways.
Wheel braking is equally effective at all speeds.

Spoilers increase drag and spoil lift, loading more weight onto the wheels.

correct_answers.text: The touchdown target zone is usually about 1,000 feet beyond the runway threshold.
Braking should begin as soon after touchdown and wheel spin-up as possible.

wrong_answers.text: The longest runway distance to stop is achieved by touching down as close to the threshold as possible.
Heavy braking is always recommended, even without an anti-skid system.
The total energy to be dissipated is greatest if there is no excess speed.
The pilot controls only the 'what' factors of stopping forces, not the 'when.'
Tire ground friction is primarily affected by air temperature.
Directional control and braking forces are independent regarding tire friction.
Maintaining a nose-high attitude during rollout significantly improves jet airplane deceleration.
Thrust reversers are most effective at low speeds.

To model after the FAA’s Master MEL for each aircraft type
To provide operational procedures for flight crews and maintenance personnel

wrong_answers.text: To list all possible equipment failures
To replace the aircraft's maintenance manual
To serve as a checklist for pre-flight inspections
To authorize all flights regardless of equipment status
To provide a list of spare parts
To ensure all equipment is operational before takeoff
To serve as a pilot's training manual

question: What must an MEL include according to 14 CFR part 91, section 91.213(a)(3)(ii)?

correct_answers.text: Provision for operation with inoperable equipment
Conditions for safe operation
Items that do not allow for safe operation are excluded

wrong_answers.text: A list of all aircraft systems
A list of all possible malfunctions

question: How is the MEL organized for quick reference?

question: Which of the following are differences a pilot should expect when transitioning from propeller-driven airplanes to jet-powered airplanes?

correct_answers.text: Engine spool up time from low power settings is longer than with propeller-driven aircraft
Swept wing stalls begin at the wingtips rather than the root
There is no propeller-induced lift when power is increased

wrong_answers.text: Engine spool up time from low power settings is shorter due to turbine efficiency
Swept wing stalls begin at the wing root and progress outward
Propeller slipstream continues to provide additional lift during power increases on jets
Descents are most efficiently performed at high power settings to maintain energy
Higher speeds allow for larger and more aggressive flight control inputs
When descending above L/DMAX, increasing speed decreases the rate of descent
Engine intake and exhaust pose no significant ground hazard on jet aircraft
It is mainly about unrelated advanced turbine transition procedures not covered in chapter summary.
